scope: Summaries of the repository’s collected work and existing research updates, not a search of every new paper. Dates on studies are separate from the date this page was edited.

prediction.description: From human activity recognition to health modeling: body signals, digital measures and models for monitoring health and predicting disease risk.

evolution.headline: Build shared recordings for testing models
evolution.change: Annotated heart-signal datasets give researchers common examples and labels to test against.
evolution.meaning: This supplies the data needed for later learning methods; it is not itself a reusable AI model.
evolution.limit: An early foundation in this collection, not a description of every study before 2021.

evolution.headline: Reuse what a model learns across datasets
evolution.change: BENDR learns patterns from unlabelled brain recordings. BIOT extends cross-dataset learning to different body signals.
evolution.meaning: Compared with the data foundation above, the reusable component is now a trained model, not just a set of recordings.
evolution.limit: Transfer to another dataset still needs testing.

evolution.headline: Learn from several signals together
evolution.change: SleepFM combines brain, heart and breathing recordings to learn reusable patterns for sleep-related tasks.
evolution.meaning: Compared with the earlier transfer examples, this study tests how several simultaneous signals can contribute to one model.
evolution.limit: The study uses sleep-lab recordings. Its results do not establish performance on everyday smartwatch data.

evolution.headline: Connect sensor readings with language
evolution.change: SensorLM links sensor sequences to text. PH-LLM studies personalised reasoning about longer wearable histories.
evolution.meaning: Alongside signal analysis, the target now includes describing and reasoning about a person's data in words.
evolution.limit: A fluent answer can still be wrong. These are research tasks, not proof of safe medical advice.

evolution.headline: Test more tasks and longer personal histories
evolution.change: SensorFM tests transfer across 35 health tasks. SOTER predicts and fills missing readings. WearableQA tests questions about histories up to 500 days.
evolution.meaning: The question becomes which tasks a reusable model can handle, and whether calculation tools help it use long records.
evolution.limit: These studies test different tasks. Their scores do not form one year-by-year accuracy ranking.

prediction.headline: Wearable AI is learning more tasks from longer health records
prediction.summary: Across SensorFM, SOTER and WearableQA, the shared direction is to reuse body-signal models and work with more personal history. The gains come from different places: training across tasks, modelling how signals change, and giving AI tools to calculate with data.
prediction.status: Our synthesis of the cited studies
prediction.use: For teams building health-data software: compare the task, data and tools, not just the model name. A good question-answering result does not prove accurate disease prediction.
prediction.takeaway: A concrete gain: WearableQA reports 51.2% correct answers without Python tools and 71.3% with them, using the same GPT-5.4 model. Tool access and computing work differ.

dimensions.answer: Reuse one trained model for several tasks
dimensions.text: SensorFM and SOTER test models on several tasks, instead of building a separate model for each use.

dimensions.answer: Use longer personal histories and larger training collections
dimensions.text: WearableQA includes up to 500 days per person. SensorFM learns from a large collection of people's sensor recordings. These are different datasets.

dimensions.answer: No new device is established by these examples
dimensions.text: The selected work changes software and data use. It does not demonstrate a new sensor or longer battery life.

dimensions.answer: Predict future readings and fill missing ones
dimensions.text: SOTER tests both tasks. Filling a gap in a recording is a different task from predicting a person's disease.

dimensions.answer: One study reports faster computation
dimensions.text: SenFlow reports up to 51 times faster model execution in its tests. This is a speed comparison, not a gain in disease-detection accuracy.

dimensions.answer: Answer questions about months of personal data
dimensions.text: WearableQA tests whether AI can use a person's long wearable history to answer questions, rather than only label a short signal segment.

stories.name: SOTER
stories.headline: One model predicts body signals and fills missing readings
stories.change: It learns relationships between signals, their timing and recurring patterns, instead of treating them as unrelated sequences.
stories.result: Across six datasets, the authors report the lowest prediction error on four using RMSE and five using MAE. These are two different error measures.
stories.before: The paper compares against general time-series models and earlier physiological models.
stories.benefit: A candidate for teams that need both prediction and missing-data handling from one model.
stories.condition: Results depend on the paper’s test settings. Some training data are hospital recordings; the tests do not establish patient benefit.

stories.name: WearableQA
stories.headline: Calculating with personal data improves AI answers
stories.change: The test contains 4,084 questions from 200 people, using wearable histories of up to 500 days.
stories.result: GPT-5.4 scores 51.2% with row-by-row text prompting and 71.3% with Python access: a gain of 20.1 percentage points.
stories.before: In the comparison, the same model reads the data without a Python tool.
stories.benefit: Helps developers test whether a health assistant can calculate from real personal records.
stories.condition: Tools and computing work change; the model version does not. These are multiple-choice answers, not diagnosis accuracy.

stories.name: SenFlow
stories.headline: Learning from sensor data with less computing time
stories.change: SenFlow trains a signal encoder together with a generator that uses flow matching, an alternative to the diffusion method used for comparison.
stories.result: The paper reports 50.4% less training time and up to 51-fold faster inference, with tests on five datasets.
stories.before: The compared diffusion approach generates outputs through repeated sampling steps.
stories.benefit: A method to investigate when training or generation cost limits a sensor-data project.
stories.condition: The speedup is an author-reported maximum under the paper’s settings, not a guaranteed speedup on every device. It does not measure patient benefit.
stories.locator: Publisher abstract; use the linked paper for timing settings

intervention.description: Use wearable data and health records to compare possible actions, design adaptive support and test treatment effects.

evolution.headline: Work out how to compare treatment choices
evolution.change: Marginal structural models address changing treatment and patient history. Later repeated-randomisation trial designs test when support helps.
evolution.meaning: The starting question is the effect of an action, not just what a prediction model expects to happen.
evolution.limit: Estimating an effect from existing records requires assumptions; a randomised trial answers a different kind of evidence question.

evolution.headline: Study the timing and sequence of actions
evolution.change: HeartSteps tests walking suggestions at repeated moments. Causal Transformer estimates outcomes under changing treatment sequences.
evolution.meaning: Compared with a single treatment choice, these examples ask when to act and how earlier decisions affect later outcomes.
evolution.limit: A model's estimated treatment response is not the same as benefit demonstrated in a trial.

evolution.headline: Use richer sensor outcomes and responsive devices
evolution.change: ADD MALTS compares patterns of wearable measurements, not just one average. InTandem adjusts musical cues to a person's walking.
evolution.meaning: Methods can retain more of the sensor record, while devices can change their output as movement changes.
evolution.limit: These are separate method and treatment studies, not a direct performance comparison.

evolution.headline: Check whether tailored advice improves health
evolution.change: myBPmyLife tests activity and food suggestions in 602 adults with hypertension. It did not improve the main blood-pressure outcome compared with control.
evolution.meaning: Adding adaptive suggestions does not guarantee the intended health benefit, even when some behaviours improve.
evolution.limit: This result concerns this intervention and population, not every adaptive health system.

evolution.headline: Separate useful feedback from proven health benefit
evolution.change: The Pace Me trial found no better main symptom outcome. The wrist-wearables review finds more consistent effects on activity than on several other health outcomes.
evolution.meaning: Together with the earlier trial, this makes the practical question clearer: which outcome improves, for whom, and at what burden?
evolution.limit: Evidence differs by outcome and study design; newer feedback is not automatically better treatment.

intervention.headline: Health feedback is becoming more adaptive, but benefit must be tested
intervention.summary: The collected work connects sensor readings to decisions about when and how to offer support. Reviews and trials show why this needs two checks: can the system adapt its actions, and do those actions improve the outcome people care about?
intervention.status: A research direction supported by reviews and trials
intervention.use: For teams building coaching or treatment systems: test the advice, timing and outcome together. More reminders or a more accurate sensor do not automatically mean better health.
intervention.takeaway: The wrist-wearable review finds more consistent benefits for physical activity than for many other health outcomes. The Long COVID messaging trial found no better main result than its comparison group.

dimensions.answer: Choose when to help based on the person's situation
dimensions.text: The review describes support that adapts to changing circumstances, rather than sending the same advice on a fixed schedule.

dimensions.answer: Combine existing study results, not new sensor recordings
dimensions.text: One review brings together 39 reviews covering 98 studies to assess the effects of wrist-wearable feedback.

dimensions.answer: The example tests advice, not a new sensor
dimensions.text: Pace Me uses wearable activity tracking to trigger messages. It does not show that changing the device alone improves health.

dimensions.answer: Send a message when activity reaches a set level
dimensions.text: Pace Me uses this trigger to send advice about managing activity and energy to people with Long COVID.

dimensions.answer: More feedback does not always improve health
dimensions.text: The review finds more consistent benefits for activity than for other outcomes. Pace Me did not improve its main symptom outcome compared with control.

dimensions.answer: Help at the right time without too many interruptions
dimensions.text: The review identifies timing and burden as problems researchers still need to solve. This is a research goal, not an available product feature.

stories.name: Review of adaptive health support
stories.headline: Choose a useful moment to offer support
stories.change: The review explains how support can adapt to a person’s changing needs and surroundings.
stories.result: It identifies continued use, burden and social context as design problems. It does not report one new performance score.
stories.before: Fixed or poorly timed support may arrive when a person cannot or will not use it.
stories.benefit: A guide for deciding what information a coaching system needs before it sends advice.
stories.condition: A review combines earlier work. Immediate responses to a message need not imply lasting health improvement.

stories.name: Pace Me trial
stories.headline: Activity-triggered messages did not improve the main outcome
stories.change: The app adds a wearable tracker and messages at set activity levels to support energy management.
stories.result: The six-month trial randomised 250 people. It found no better main result for symptoms after exertion than the comparison group.
stories.before: The comparison app provided data-entry screens rather than the tracker-linked support package.
stories.benefit: A useful test case for checking whether sensing-linked advice adds benefit, not just features.
stories.condition: The final per-protocol analysis included 161 people. The finding applies to this Long COVID intervention, not all health messaging.
stories.locator: Abstract: design, participant counts and primary outcome

stories.name: Review of wrist-wearable health effects
stories.headline: Activity benefits are clearer than wider health benefits
stories.change: The authors combine 39 systematic reviews covering 98 original studies of wearable-based feedback.
stories.result: Physical activity increased more consistently. Effects on several other outcomes were limited or inconsistent.
stories.before: Individual studies test different devices, support packages and outcomes, making isolated results hard to compare.
stories.benefit: Helps teams choose a specific outcome to test instead of promising a broad health improvement.
stories.condition: Most included reviews had low confidence ratings, and comparison groups differed. This is not a ranking of devices.

twin.description: Models of an individual's changing physiology, updated with personal data to simulate possible trajectories and treatment choices.

evolution.headline: Test a personal model inside insulin treatment
evolution.change: A trial tests digital-twin-supported experimentation as part of automated insulin delivery.
evolution.meaning: The model is studied within a treatment system, rather than as a stand-alone prediction demo.
evolution.limit: This is a diabetes-specific example. The column has too few primary records for a broad historical trend.

evolution.headline: Update personal feedback and propose treatment comparisons
evolution.change: A small type 2 diabetes study retrains models weekly and sends daily feedback. A separate causal-twin paper proposes how to compare possible actions.
evolution.meaning: Compared with the 2025 insulin example, the collection adds a different diabetes-care use and a framework for treatment reasoning.
evolution.limit: The studies concern different systems and populations; this does not establish improvement over the 2025 trial. The causal framework is not a clinical result.

twin.headline: Personal models are being tested for feedback and treatment decisions
twin.summary: The concrete examples link a model of one person to repeated feedback or treatment adjustment. The common direction is a model that keeps being used and updated, rather than a one-time prediction. The evidence here remains specific to diabetes.
twin.status: Our comparison of disease-specific studies and a proposed method
twin.use: For teams building personal models: specify what the model represents, how often it updates and which decision it supports. Test that decision before calling the system a complete digital twin.
twin.takeaway: The 2026 study updates models weekly and sends daily feedback, but includes only 19 people. Earlier insulin-delivery work provides a separate trial example; it is not an October 2026 breakthrough.

dimensions.answer: Update the personal model as new data arrives
dimensions.text: The 2026 type 2 diabetes study retrains each person's model weekly, instead of leaving it unchanged after its initial training.

dimensions.answer: A small study of 19 people
dimensions.text: This is the group analysed in the newer diabetes study, not a large new public dataset for general personal-health models.

dimensions.answer: Use a personal model within an insulin-delivery system
dimensions.text: The 2025 trial studies model-supported treatment adjustment. It is not evidence of a new general-purpose body sensor.

dimensions.answer: Give daily feedback between care visits
dimensions.text: The 2026 study combines weekly model updates with daily text messages. This is one diabetes-care example, not the full scope of personal models.

dimensions.answer: Weight outcomes differed; glucose stayed stable
dimensions.text: The small 2026 study reports these outcomes for its two groups. It does not show that all personal-health models improve care.

dimensions.answer: Estimate what a different treatment might change
dimensions.text: The causal-twin paper proposes a framework for comparing choices. It has not demonstrated a working simulator of an entire person.

stories.name: Type 2 diabetes predictive twin
stories.headline: Weekly model updates support daily personal feedback
stories.change: Personal models are retrained weekly and generate daily text-message suggestions, with nurse-scored safeguards.
stories.result: The analysis includes 19 people: 10 in the AI group and 9 in the comparison group. Weight outcomes differed; glucose stayed stable.
stories.before: The comparison uses self-monitoring and periodic care without model-generated daily feedback.
stories.benefit: Shows one way to connect a personal model with support between visits.
stories.condition: This small, single-centre study does not establish better glucose control or a full real-time model of the body.
stories.locator: Methods: participant selection and model updates; results

stories.name: Twin-supported insulin-delivery trial
stories.headline: Test the personal model inside a treatment system
stories.change: Individual glucose–insulin models support treatment adjustment as part of a larger care package.
stories.result: The repository’s source review reports 72 participants over six months and improved time in the target glucose range for the full package.
stories.before: The study compares twin-guided adjustment with conventional feedback around automated insulin delivery.
stories.benefit: An earlier example of evaluating an action supported by the model, rather than only prediction accuracy.
stories.condition: This summary relies on the repository’s 4 Oct source review; the publisher page could not be reopened in this check. The trial concerns type 1 diabetes and the full package, not an unrestricted body simulator.
stories.verification: Existing source review retained; original page could not be reopened in this check

stories.name: Causal digital-twin proposal
stories.headline: Ask what a different treatment would change
stories.change: The proposal connects personal models with methods for comparing alternative actions over time.
stories.result: It offers a design framework, not a new dataset or a clinical performance result.
stories.before: A model that predicts a person’s future does not by itself show the effect of changing treatment.
stories.benefit: A checklist for separating prediction from action claims in personal-model projects.
stories.condition: Summarised from the existing reviewed repository entry. Assumptions about cause and effect still need to be checked in each application.
stories.locator: Existing repository entry and source review
stories.verification: Existing source review retained; original paper not rechecked in this pass

interface.description: Wearable sensing, body input and mixed reality as potential ways to display and interact with a personal digital twin.

evolution.headline: Build datasets for brain and muscle controls
evolution.change: Motor-imagery and hand-movement datasets support testing interfaces driven by brain or muscle recordings. MOABB makes brain-interface comparisons more consistent.
evolution.meaning: These resources make controlled comparisons possible before claiming that an interface works across users.
evolution.limit: A benchmark is not a finished wearable product.

evolution.headline: Include what the wearer sees in daily life
evolution.change: Ego4D provides videos recorded from the wearer's viewpoint during everyday activities.
evolution.meaning: Alongside body-signal controls, researchers can study actions in their visual surroundings.
evolution.limit: This is another research branch, not a replacement for brain or muscle sensing.

evolution.headline: Link viewpoints and record detailed hand actions
evolution.change: Ego-Exo4D pairs wearer and outside views. emg2pose and emg2qwerty provide wrist-muscle data for hand pose and typing.
evolution.meaning: The data support more detailed questions than which broad activity or gesture occurred.
evolution.limit: Dataset access does not by itself demonstrate a reliable interface in everyday use.

evolution.headline: Train muscle controls across people and tasks
evolution.change: The generic neuromotor-interface study trains a noninvasive muscle-signal model across users and interaction tasks.
evolution.meaning: Compared with collecting labelled movements, the focus is now how widely one control model can be reused.
evolution.limit: Performance still depends on the task, device and user conditions that were tested.

evolution.headline: Try optical muscle controls and open glasses app tools
evolution.change: An optical wristband tests continuous cursor control using light-based muscle sensing. Meta announces supported tools for connecting apps to AI glasses.
evolution.meaning: One branch changes the sensing hardware; another gives developers access to device functions. They are different kinds of progress.
evolution.limit: The optical interface is a small research study. Glasses features have separate rollout and preview conditions.

interface.headline: Wearables are gaining new body controls and more app-building tools
interface.summary: Two related developments stand out: research uses muscle signals for continuous device control, while glasses makers expose more inputs to apps. Together they suggest more ways to interact without a handheld controller. Research tests and product availability remain separate questions.
interface.status: Our synthesis of sensor research and company announcements
interface.use: For interface teams: separate input accuracy, user calibration and app access. A working research sensor and an announced software toolkit are different levels of readiness.
interface.takeaway: The optical wristband study tested nine people. Meta’s September toolkit update is a company-announced release, not an independent test showing better accuracy or longer battery life.

dimensions.answer: Use muscle signals for continuous device control
dimensions.text: The interface studies examine controls such as moving a cursor, rather than only recognising a fixed set of separate gestures.

dimensions.answer: An earlier dataset links wearer and outside views
dimensions.text: Ego-Exo4D records the same activity from different viewpoints. It supports this research but is not a new 2026 dataset.

dimensions.answer: A research wristband reads muscle movement using light
dimensions.text: The optical wristband uses 50 recording channels. It is a research prototype, not a confirmed retail-device upgrade.

dimensions.answer: Let mobile apps use glasses and body inputs
dimensions.text: Meta announced an app-development toolkit. Some related tools are still in preview or early access, so availability must be checked feature by feature.

dimensions.answer: Small user tests, not a consumer-device ranking
dimensions.text: Nine participants learned the optical wristband controls. This does not establish better accuracy or battery life than retail devices.

dimensions.answer: Build apps that use glasses and body movements
dimensions.text: The announced tools give developers another way to receive user input. They do not by themselves create a personal health model.

stories.name: Meta Wearables Device Access Toolkit
stories.date: Rollout announced for 30 Sep 2026 · company news
stories.headline: A supported toolkit for building glasses apps
stories.change: Meta announced a supported release after its developer-preview period, with app access to glasses and body inputs.
stories.result: This changes what developers can connect to apps. It is an availability announcement, not a measured performance gain.
stories.before: Earlier integrations relied on a developer-preview toolkit and testing mode.
stories.benefit: Relevant to mobile teams exploring hands-free app interactions.
stories.condition: WebMCP is still preview, connectors are early access and discovery is described as coming soon. Check each feature separately.
stories.locator: Device Access Toolkit section and rollout notice

stories.name: Optical muscle-sensing wristband
stories.headline: Use light-based muscle sensing for cursor control
stories.change: A 50-channel wristband and a small neural network translate muscle activity into computer controls.
stories.result: Eight participants without limb loss and one participant with limb loss learned cursor tasks and Tetris controls.
stories.before: The study investigates an optical alternative to skin electrodes that read muscle electrical activity.
stories.benefit: A prototype to study for continuous hands-free control and alternative sensor design.
stories.condition: Users need calibration and training. This small study does not prove a retail-device upgrade or a general speed advantage over every electrical sensor.
stories.locator: Abstract and Figure 1: hardware, calibration and participants

stories.name: Ego-Exo4D
stories.headline: Study the same activity from the wearer and outside cameras
stories.change: Paired recordings connect what a person sees with their actions in the surrounding scene.
stories.result: The repository lists more than 1,400 hours. This is a data resource, not a new glasses function.
stories.before: A single camera view does not show both the wearer’s view and the full external scene.
stories.benefit: Useful background data for teams studying movements in context.
stories.condition: This summary uses the existing repository entry, not a newly checked data release. Read the dataset’s access terms before reuse.
stories.locator: Existing dataset entry: scale, contribution and access
stories.verification: Repository entry read; original dataset site not rechecked in this pass
